newsitem.title: CROATIA: Croatia's Tudjman in spotlight as election called.
newsitem.headline: Croatia's Tudjman in spotlight as election called.

text.p: Croatian President Franjo Tudjman is expected to romp to re-election next month but the spotlight has fallen again on his questionable role in the bloody breakup of the former Yugoslavia.
The Croatian government on Monday set June 15 as the date for elections in which Tudjman has said he will run as candidate for the Croatian Democratic Union (HDZ), seeking another five-year term.

Reported to be seriously ill, Tudjman, who will be 75 on Wednesday, enjoys widespread popularity in Croatia and is likely to be re-elected easily despite allegations of corruption and authoritarianism within his party.

A statement issued at the weekend by his medical team said his health was excellent. But diplomats and other independent observers say he has been battling cancer since last year and is unlikely to last another term.
Tudjman is known as the "Father of the Nation" for declaring Croatian independence in 1991. He then led his country in a bitter war which spread throughout ex-Yugoslavia.
He was elected as the first president of independent Croatia on August 2, 1992 with 56 percent of the vote.
His role in Bosnia's war has never been clarified and fresh press controversy last week again raised the issue.

A political row involving the international war crimes tribunal in The Hague blew up when newspaper stories tried to portray an opposition politician as a traitor who had criticised Tudjman in interviews with tribunal officials.
But the row also backfired somewhat and served to revive questions about whether Tudjman planned to carve up Bosnia with Serbia's President Slobodan Milosevic.
Tudjman has never suffered the same opprobrium as Milosevic and his country escaped international sanctions unlike former fellow Yugoslav republics Serbia and Montenegro.
Croatia has clear aspirations towards the West and refuses to accept being labelled as part of the Balkans which it views as a backward, unstable region.
But its ambition to join West European institutions has been set back by slow progress on human rights questions and media freedom under the conservative nationalist HDZ.

If re-elected, Tudjman must improve Croatia's handling of such issues to move forward with talks on a cooperation agreement with the European Union and to ensure loans are not blocked by critical Western countries, analysts say.

The top U.N. official in Croatia, Jacques Klein, slammed Tudjman last week for treatment of minority Serb refugees, and the coordinated release of leaked Hague tribunal documents in several papers showed how strong government influence is.
Tudjman will face a disunited opposition in June and there has even been suggestions of a boycott by rival parties to render hollow another victory by the president.
Liberal leader Vlado Gotovac may try the impossible and run against Tudjman but has said there is no point if the opposition does not have fair access to the media.
"This would represent fighting a battle that has already been lost," he told independent satirical weekly Feral Tribune.
He said he would be ready to join a boycott if other candidates agreed.
Another idea being thrown around opposition circles is running a joint candidate to represent several leftist parties.
But it is believed more candidates could take some votes away from Tudjman and force him to enter a second round, only needed if he fails to secure an outright majority in the first.
